For further reading on the subject of generational cynicism: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strauss%E2%80%93Howe_generational_theory

Strauss and Howe's book, Generations, was published in 1991. I have read it multiple times and it is highly enlightening. It is a bit dated now but it definitely explains a lot regarding why different generations act they way they do. Their theory is that there are four types of generations that continually cycle throughout history.

According to the book: * Generation X is referred to as a Nomad (Reactive) generation. They assign the birth years as 1961–1981. * Millennial Generation is referred to as a Hero (Civic) generation. They assign the birth years as 1982–2004.

Nomad Nomad generations are born during an Awakening, a time of social ideals and spiritual agendas, when young adults are passionately attacking the established institutional order. Nomads grow up as under-protected children during this Awakening, come of age as alienated, post-Awakening adults, become pragmatic midlife leaders during a Crisis, and age into resilient post-Crisis elders.

Hero Hero generations are born after an Awakening, during an Unraveling, a time of individual pragmatism, self-reliance, and laissez faire. Heroes grow up as increasingly protected post-Awakening children, come of age as team-oriented young optimists during a Crisis, emerge as energetic, overly-confident midlifers, and age into politically powerful elders attacked by another Awakening.

People who were children during the 80's would include late Generation X and early Millennial Generation. The early onset of cynicism is an aspect of Generation X as well as those early Millennials who identify somewhat with Generation X.

Hah....that sounds pretty neat, I haven't heard about them. It definitely seems like something worth checking out; I wonder how 9/11 might have changed any of their views. [which could be an interesting topic in itself]

IIRC, their cycle theory predicted a Crisis event like a 9/11. However, the event occurred a few years earlier than predicted and may have altered the generational cycle in America. Either that or there is some other Crisis which awaits us.

According to their theory, there was one time in US history where the cycle skipped a generation, and that was as a result of the devastation of the Civil War.

The book is divided into three sections. The first explains their theory. The second goes through each generation one-by-one, starting from 1584. The third offers their predictions for the future, as of 1991. I seem to remember the first section reintroducing and repeating their main thesis multiple times. If it gets to be too long of a read, feel free to skip the rest of the first section after you get the hang of what they are saying. The second section was my favorite part, it put the whole idea of generations throughout history more into focus. The third section is a little theoretical and harder to digest, as they did not have actual events to write about. Like I said before, I've read the book multiple times, but I don't always make it through the third section. If you end up reading it, I hope you enjoy it!

Well think of it this way. Our parents' generation had a much more idealistic and scripted life path than ours. Close affinity to families, 'christian values', small town where everyone knows each other, etc. Not only that, but the economy was in much better shape, people had more spending money, there were more (and this is the important part) high paying jobs, a reason to get a degree and settle down, and much less overall confusion as to what to do with life.

Our generation, from the 80s to the millenials, is known as the post-enlightenment era. We have, and are more accustomed to, a wider variety of sociopolitical, economic, and technological changes, and as such, have a much easier time adapting, and by extension, better abstract thought skills. We think more about our place in the universe, how our actions impact the world, how we value life, the list goes on and on.

That kind of thinking is conducive to 'cynicism' as the western world knows it. It's not the true definition of cynicism, it's much closer to rationality than idealism. We don't force ourselves to think only positive, we take the good with the bad, and try to better process and understand it.
